html:
The Beothuk were an Indigenous people of the island of Newfoundland. Their culture as known to history formed around 1500. The last known Beothuk, a woman named Shanawdithit, died in 1829.

Their ancestors came over from Labrador around 1 CE and went through three earlier cultural phases, each lasting about 500 years; the one just before the Beothuk appears on this map as Boethuk. The Beothuk hunted caribou in the interior in winter and took seals, fish, birds and eggs on the coast in summer. They travelled in birchbark canoes of a distinctive crescent shape, and coated their bodies and belongings with red ochre, which may be where Europeans got the term "Red Indians".

The Norse who landed at L'Anse aux Meadows around 1000 may have met their ancestors. From 1497, when John Cabot reached the island, European fishermen came every summer. Unlike most peoples of the region, the Beothuk mostly avoided trade, taking iron by scavenging from empty fishing stations instead. As English settlement spread around the coast, they lost the shore and its food. Hunger, disease and killings by settlers wore them down, and relations with the Mi'kmaq, who also came to the island, were often hostile.

Their neighbours across the Strait of Belle Isle were the Innu. Much of what we know of Beothuk life comes from drawings and words Shanawdithit gave to her captors in her last years.
sum: The Beothuk were an Indigenous people of the island of Newfoundland. Their culture as known to history formed around 1500. The last known Beothuk, a woman named Shanawdithit, died in 1829.
